overview.title: 📖 Overview: From Shifting Words to a New Chapter on Cooking
overview.subtitle: Shabbat 36a–36b
overview.hebrewSource: כִּירָה שֶׁהִסִּיקוּהָ בְּקַשׁ וּבִגְבָבָא — נוֹתְנִים עָלֶיהָ תַּבְשִׁיל
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: The daf closes out the discussion of moving a shofar or trumpet with a short excursus on how Hebrew and Aramaic terms drifted after the Temple's destruction — with real halakhic stakes for shofar-blowing, the four species, commerce, kashrut, and even bills of divorce. The first chapter then ends, and a new chapter opens with a fresh mishna: the laws of a stove (keirah) heated before Shabbat, and whether cooked food may be placed, left, or returned to it. Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel disagree, and the Gemara opens a basic question about how to read the mishna's very first line.

callout.label: Why this matters:
callout.text: Halakha often hinges on precise terminology — a mistaken word can invalidate a lulav, a get, or a kashrut ruling.

slides.title: 🍲 New Mishna: What May Sit on the Stove Before Shabbat
slides.subtitle: Chapter 3 opens with the laws of a keirah (stove)

steps.content: 1️⃣ Stove lit with straw or rakings (quick-burning fuel): a pot of cooked food may be placed on it, since the fire is certainly out by Shabbat
2️⃣ Stove lit with pomace or wood (long-burning fuel): nothing may be placed until the coals are swept out or covered with ash
3️⃣ Beit Shammai: even after sweeping, only hot water may be placed — not cooked food
4️⃣ Beit Hillel: both hot water and cooked food may be placed
5️⃣ Beit Shammai: a pot may be removed from the stove on Shabbat, but not returned
6️⃣ Beit Hillel: a pot may even be returned to the stove on Shabbat

slides.title: 🤔 What Does 'He May Not Place' Actually Mean?
slides.subtitle: The Gemara's opening dilemma on the mishna's very first line

lines.speaker: Option A
lines.text: 'He may not place' means he may not return a pot once removed. But leaving a pot from before Shabbat is fine — even on an unswept stove — since it was already cooking.

lines.speaker: Source
lines.text: This matches Chananya's view: any food cooked to the level of מַאֲכַל בֶּן דְּרוּסַאי ('ben Drosai's food' — minimally cooked) may be left on an unswept stove.

lines.speaker: Option B
lines.text: Or perhaps 'he may not place' means one may not even leave a pot on an unswept stove from before Shabbat — and returning one on Shabbat is certainly worse.

lines.speaker: Stakes
lines.text: Under this reading, sweeping or ashing the coals is required just to leave food on the stove overnight, not only to return it.

slides.title: 🔍 Testing the Two Readings Against the Mishna's Structure
slides.subtitle: An attempted proof from the mishna's two matching disputes

nodes.content: ❓ The mishna records two Beit Shammai/Beit Hillel disputes back to back — hot water vs. cooked food, then remove vs. return
💡 If the mishna's opening means 'leaving': the first dispute (what may be left) and the second (what may be returned) read as two separate, parallel questions — a clean fit
🤨 If the opening means 'returning': the second dispute about returning becomes redundant, since the first already covered it
⚖️ Neither reading is fully proven yet — the Gemara's inquiry continues

callout.label: Still open:
callout.text: The proof from the mishna's parallel structure favors 'leaving,' but the Gemara has not yet closed the question.

slides.title: 🍳 Chananya's Standard: 'Ben Drosai's Food'
slides.subtitle: The minimal cooking threshold that anchors one side of the debate
slides.label: The practical marker:
slides.text: Chananya teaches that any food cooked to the extent that a legendary quick-cooking bandit named ben Drosai would consider done — the bare minimum for edibility — may be left on an unswept stove into Shabbat, since it needs no further cooking and there is no worry that someone will stoke the coals. This standard becomes the practical yardstick throughout the coming discussion for distinguishing food that still needs the fire from food that does not.

summary.principle: Precise language matters in halakha — shifting word-meanings can change how a mitzva or a legal document is fulfilled — and the new chapter's opening question, whether 'he may not place' means 'return' or 'leave,' will shape every ruling about cooking on Shabbat that follows.

quiz.q: According to Rav Chisda, which pair of terms swapped meaning since the Temple's destruction, with consequences for Rosh Hashana?
o: Willow and tzaftzafa
Trumpet and shofar
Large table and small table
Babylon and Bursif
quiz.e: Rav Chisda taught that what was once called trumpet became known as shofar and vice versa — relevant to which instrument fulfills the Rosh Hashana mitzva.

quiz.q: What halakhic issue does Abaye's addition about huvlila and bei kasei (the two stomachs) affect?
o: Whether an animal may be eaten on Yom Kippur
Whether a needle found in the stomach wall renders the animal a tereifa
The laws of tithing animals
The size of a kosher sukkah
quiz.e: Abaye notes the names of the first and second stomach also swapped, which matters for whether a needle puncturing the wall makes the animal a tereifa.

quiz.q: In the new mishna about a stove (keirah), what does Beit Shammai permit placing on a swept, pomace-or-wood-heated stove?
o: Only cooked food, not hot water
Both hot water and cooked food
Neither hot water nor cooked food
Only hot water, not cooked food
quiz.e: Beit Shammai permits only hot water on such a stove; Beit Hillel permits both hot water and cooked food.

quiz.q: What is the Gemara's opening dilemma about the mishna's phrase 'he may not place' (lo yitein)?
o: Whether it applies only to meat dishes
Whether it means 'may not return' a removed pot, or 'may not even leave' a pot from before Shabbat
Whether it applies only on Yom Tov
Whether it refers to bread or to stew
quiz.e: The Gemara asks whether the prohibition is limited to returning a pot already removed, or extends to leaving a pot on an unswept stove in the first place.

quiz.q: What is Chananya's 'ben Drosai' standard used to determine?
o: The minimum size of a kosher stove
The point at which food is cooked enough to be left on an unswept stove without concern
The exact time Shabbat begins
How much water is needed to insulate a pot
quiz.e: Chananya holds that food cooked to the minimal 'ben Drosai' level may be left on an unswept, uncovered stove, since no one would need to stoke the coals further.
